lessons.title: Day 1 · Expressions and Equivalent Forms
lessons.body:
ALGEBRA I • UNIT 1 • DAY 1 OF 5 • 55 MINUTES
Essential question: What makes two algebraic expressions equivalent?
Learning targets: I can distinguish expressions from equations; evaluate expressions using substitution; use distribution and collecting like terms to rewrite expressions. Standards: HSA-SSE.A.1; HSA-REI.A.1. Prerequisites: signed-number operations and the order of operations.

LAUNCH (5 min)
A school club orders 3 shirts for each of n volunteers, plus 6 extras. Two students represent the shirts as 3n + 6 and 3(n + 2). Try n = 4 and n = 10. Are the expressions equal for every n? Explain using distribution, not only a calculator.

EXPLICIT INSTRUCTION (12 min)
A variable represents a quantity. An expression such as 4x - 5 has no equality claim; an equation such as 4x - 5 = 19 asserts equality. Terms are quantities joined by addition or subtraction. Like terms share the same variable part (5x and -2x), so 5x - 2x + 7 = 3x + 7. Distribute: 2(3x - 4) = 6x - 8. The expressions 2(3x - 4) and 6x - 8 are equivalent for every x.
WORKED EXAMPLE: Simplify 4(2x - 3) - (x + 5).
1. Distribute: 8x - 12 - x - 5.
2. Combine like terms: 7x - 17.
3. Check with x = 2: original 4(4 - 3) - (2 + 5) = 4 - 7 = -3; simplified 14 - 17 = -3.
Checking one input helps catch errors; using distribution and like terms establishes equivalence.

GUIDED PRACTICE (12 min)
A. Evaluate 2a + 3b for a = -2 and b = 5; show substituted expression first.
B. Simplify 5(y + 2) - 3y.
C. Explain why 4x + 4 cannot be simplified to 8x.
Compare reasoning with a peer or teacher; explicitly name the equality property used.

INDEPENDENT PRACTICE (16 min)
1. Evaluate 3x² - 2x for x = -2.
2. Expand and simplify 3(2p - 5) + 4p.
3. Write two different equivalent expressions for the cost of n $8 tickets with a one-time $6 fee.
4. Error analysis: A student rewrites 2(x + 5) as 2x + 5. Identify the mistake and fix it.
5. Challenge: Show algebraically that (x + 3) + (2x - 4) equals 3x - 1 for every real x.

EXIT TICKET (10 min)
Simplify 2(3k - 4) + k and explain each step. Then write one sentence describing the difference between an expression and an equation.
Turn in the exit ticket for formative feedback; it is not a grade from lesson completion alone.

SELF-CHECK AND SUPPORT
For guided practice: A = 11; B = 2y + 10; C combines unlike terms. If you distributed to obtain 2x + 5, revisit how multiplication applies to every term inside parentheses. Extension: design two equivalent formulas for a school fundraiser.

lessons.title: Day 2 · Solving Equations with Equality
lessons.body:
ALGEBRA I • UNIT 1 • DAY 2 OF 5 • 55 MINUTES
Essential question: Why does doing the same operation to both sides preserve equality?
Learning targets: I can solve one- and two-step equations, justify each transformation, and check solutions. Standards: HSA-REI.A.1, HSA-REI.B.3.
Materials: pencil, scratch paper or equation editor. Prior knowledge: inverse operations.

LAUNCH (6 min)
A balance scale holds a sealed bag and 7 blocks on the left, 19 blocks on the right. What is the mass of the bag in block units? Write b + 7 = 19. Explain what happens if we remove 7 blocks from both sides.

MINI-LESSON (12 min)
An equation gives two equal quantities. Subtracting, adding, multiplying or dividing by the same nonzero quantity on both sides preserves the solution set. To isolate x in 3x + 5 = 20:
1. Subtract 5 on each side: 3x = 15.
2. Divide each side by 3: x = 5.
3. Substitute into the original: 3(5) + 5 = 20. Both sides equal 20.
A calculation without a check can conceal sign mistakes. In -2x - 6 = 10, add 6 then divide by -2 to get x = -8. Substitute: -2(-8) - 6 = 10.

GUIDED REASONING (12 min)
1. Solve x - 9 = -2, naming the inverse operation.
2. Solve 4y + 6 = -10. Which operation comes first and why?
3. A peer claims 5x = 20 gives x = 100. Explain the incorrect inverse and correct it.
4. Solve (t/3) - 2 = 4. Check by substitution.

INDEPENDENT PRACTICE (15 min)
A. 7n - 3 = 25.
B. -3m + 4 = 19.
C. 5 + p/2 = -1.
D. Translate and solve: A membership costs a $12 signup fee plus $6 for each visit. A total bill is $48. How many visits? Explain why visits must be a whole number here.
E. Write a two-step equation with solution x = -4 and show a valid solution pathway.

EXIT TICKET (10 min)
Solve -4x + 7 = 23, label each equality-preserving operation and confirm your solution in the original equation.

SELF-CHECK
Guided: 1 = 7; 2 = -4; 4 = 18. Independent: A = 4; B = -5; C = -12; D = 6 visits. The exit ticket solution is x = -4. If a check fails, retrace the first transformation where equality stopped being preserved.

lessons.title: Day 3 · Distributive and Multi-Step Equations
lessons.body:
ALGEBRA I • UNIT 1 • DAY 3 OF 5 • 55 MINUTES
Essential question: How can we solve equations that contain parentheses and variables on both sides?
Learning targets: I can distribute, gather variable terms, detect contradictions and identities, and explain why an equation may have one, no, or infinitely many solutions. Standards: HSA-REI.A.1 and HSA-REI.B.3.

WARM-UP (5 min)
Simplify 2(3x - 4) and 4x + 2x - 8. Are they equivalent? What is the difference between simplifying an expression and solving an equation?

TEACHING AND WORKED EXAMPLES (15 min)
Example 1: 3(2x - 1) = x + 12.
Distribute: 6x - 3 = x + 12.
Subtract x: 5x - 3 = 12.
Add 3: 5x = 15.
Divide by 5: x = 3.
Verify: 3(6 - 1) = 15 and 3 + 12 = 15.
Example 2: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6. Distribute: 2x + 6 = 2x + 6. Every real x works, so infinitely many solutions.
Example 3: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 5. Distribute and subtract 2x: 6 = 5. This is false, so there is no solution.
A zero coefficient does not automatically mean x = 0; read the remaining statement.

GUIDED WORK (10 min)
A. Solve 4x + 9 = 2x - 3 and explain each step.
B. Solve 5(y - 2) = 2y + 8.
C. Classify 3(x + 2) = 3x + 7 without guessing a value.
D. Classify 4(z - 1) = 4z - 4. Describe what the final statement means.

INDEPENDENT PRACTICE (15 min)
1. Solve 2(3p + 1) = 4p + 12 and check.
2. Solve 7 - 2a = 3(a + 4).
3. Classify 6(t + 1) - 2 = 6t + 4.
4. Construct an equation that has no solution and one that has infinitely many; use the same variable on both sides.
5. A student subtracts 3x from one side only in 5x + 4 = 3x + 10. Explain the error and give a correct solution.

EXIT TICKET (10 min)
Classify 5(x - 2) + 1 = 5x - 9 and solve 3(x + 4) = x - 2. Show reasoning, not just a final number.

SELF-CHECK
Guided: A = -6; B = 6; C no solution; D infinitely many solutions. Independent: 1 = 5; 2 = -1; 3 infinitely many. Exit: first equation is an identity; second solution x = -7. Seek help if you are unsure why 0 = 0 means every number works.
learningTargets: I can distribute, gather variable terms, detect contradictions and identities, and explain why an equation may have one, no, or infinitely many solutions. Standards: HSA-REI.A.1 and HSA-REI.B.3.

lessons.title: Day 4 · Inequalities and Their Solution Sets
lessons.body:
ALGEBRA I • UNIT 1 • DAY 4 OF 5 • 55 MINUTES
Essential question: How do inequalities describe ranges of possible answers?
Learning targets: I can solve one-variable linear inequalities, reverse the comparison when multiplying or dividing by a negative, and represent solutions in words and on a number line. Standard: HSA-REI.B.3 and HSA-CED.A.1.

CONTEXT (6 min)
A club may spend at most $50. Room rental is $14 and each participant costs $4. Write 14 + 4n ≤ 50. What values of n make sense? Algebra says n ≤ 9; in this setting n is a nonnegative whole number.

MINI-LESSON (12 min)
An inequality such as x < 7 describes many values. For x + 3 ≤ 8, subtract 3 from both sides: x ≤ 5. A number line uses a closed dot at 5 and shading to the left.
CAUTION WITH NEGATIVES: Solve -3x > 12. Divide both sides by -3 AND reverse > to <: x < -4. Why? Multiplying an inequality by -1 reverses order: because 2 < 5, -2 > -5.
Check boundary and samples: x = -5 satisfies -3(-5) > 12, because 15 > 12. x = -3 does not.

GUIDED PRACTICE (12 min)
1. Solve 2x - 1 ≥ 9, and state if x = 5 is included.
2. Solve -2y + 3 < 11, explaining the sign reversal.
3. Describe an open dot at -1 shaded right using inequality symbols.
4. Sketch the interval x ≥ -2 in words if a visual number line is unavailable.

INDEPENDENT PRACTICE (15 min)
A. 7 + 3t ≤ 22.
B. -4n ≥ 16.
C. 5 - 2p > 13.
D. Write a real-life constraint using an inequality. Solve it and describe the domain (all reals, whole numbers, etc.).
E. Error analysis: someone divides -2x < 8 by -2 and writes x < -4. Diagnose and correct the mistake.

EXIT TICKET (10 min)
Solve -5x + 2 ≥ 17. State if x = -3 is included. Explain one way an inequality differs from an equation.

SELF-CHECK
Guided 1: x ≥ 5, yes. 2: y > -4. 3: x > -1. Independent A: t ≤ 5; B: n ≤ -4; C: p < -4; E: x > -4. Exit: x ≤ -3, and -3 is included. If unsure about a boundary, substitute it into the original inequality.
learningTargets: I can solve one-variable linear inequalities, reverse the comparison when multiplying or dividing by a negative, and represent solutions in words and on a number line. Standard: HSA-REI.B.3 and HSA-CED.A.1.

lessons.title: Day 5 · Modeling and Evidence of Mastery
lessons.body:
ALGEBRA I • UNIT 1 • DAY 5 OF 5 • 55 MINUTES
Essential question: How do we translate an unfamiliar situation into an equation or inequality and defend the answer?
Learning targets: I can define variables, create a linear equation or inequality from a context, solve accurately, check feasibility, and explain my reasoning. Standards: HSA-CED.A.1, HSA-REI.A.1, HSA-REI.B.3.

LAUNCH (5 min)
A school has $150 for an after-school science event. The venue charges $30 and each lab kit costs $8. Write an equation to find exactly how many kits $150 buys, then determine how many kits are affordable if spending must stay at or below $150. Is it possible to buy half a kit?

WORKED MODEL (12 min)
Let k be the number of kits. Define k as a nonnegative integer.
Budget model: 30 + 8k ≤ 150.
Subtract 30: 8k ≤ 120.
Divide by 8: k ≤ 15.
Conclusion: The school can purchase at most 15 kits. Check: 30 + 8(15) = 150. If k = 16, cost would be $158, too high. The domain matters: negative or fractional numbers of kits are not permitted.

GUIDED TRANSFER (12 min)
1. A student has $42 and wants notebooks at $5 each after paying a $7 delivery charge. Model, solve and interpret.
2. A subscription costs $11 plus $3 for each extra class. Total charged is $29. Model and solve.
3. A museum ticket costs $9 and 5 tickets cost $45. Is 5(9) = 45 an expression or equation? Explain.

INDEPENDENT PRACTICE (15 min)
A. Create an equation from: four times a number minus 7 equals 29. Solve and check.
B. Create an inequality from: at least 20 minutes of exercise have been completed, and every round adds 6 minutes, starting from 8 minutes. Find the minimum whole number of rounds needed.
C. Invent a school-business constraint using a fixed fee and per-student cost. Define variables, solve and critique one assumption in your model.
D. Explain why an accurate algebraic solution sometimes needs to be rounded down and sometimes up based on context.

UNIT REFLECTION AND NEXT STEPS (11 min)
Review your work from Days 1–4. Identify a strength and an error you corrected. Complete the Unit 1 Checkpoint assignment in your class's Assignments view. Attach no personal information in mathematical examples. The checkpoint is scored by your teacher; clicking 'Mark lesson complete' records instructional progress but does not confer academic credit.

SELF-CHECK
Guided 1: 7 + 5n ≤ 42, so n ≤ 7 whole notebooks. 2: 11 + 3c = 29, c = 6. Independent A: n = 9. B: 8 + 6r ≥ 20 gives r ≥ 2. For C, check whether the cost rule is realistic and whether quantities must be whole numbers.
learningTargets: I can define variables, create a linear equation or inequality from a context, solve accurately, check feasibility, and explain my reasoning. Standards: HSA-CED.A.1, HSA-REI.A.1, HSA-REI.B.3.

assessments.title: Algebra I · Unit 1 Guided Problem Set
assessments.instructions:
UNIT 1 GUIDED PROBLEM SET • 20 POINTS • Submit work as text.
Explain each transformation and use the equal sign correctly. Teacher feedback guides revisions.
1. Simplify 4(2x - 3) - (x + 5). Explain two algebraic rules you used.
2. Solve 3(2x - 1) = x + 12 and verify by substitution.
3. Solve -2y + 3 < 11; explain why the inequality symbol changes or does not change.
4. A field trip charges $15 per student plus a fixed bus fee of $90. Total is $285. Define a variable, write and solve an equation for the number of students; check that the result makes sense.
Write numbered responses, include units when relevant, and explain how you checked your answers.

rubricCriteria.label: Define variables and build an equation or inequality
rubricCriteria.description: Quantity definitions and accurate mathematical model.

rubricCriteria.label: Solve with justified steps
rubricCriteria.description: Valid inverse operations, accurate algebra and written reasoning.

assessments.title: Algebra I · Unit 1 Mastery Checkpoint
assessments.instructions:
UNIT 1 CHECKPOINT • 30 POINTS • Individual written assessment.
Show your own steps and explanation. You may use ordinary scratch paper; enter the solution and reasoning in your submission.
1 (5 pts). Simplify 3(2a - 5) + 4a. Evaluate your result for a = 2 and verify against the original expression.
2 (5 pts). Solve 5(2x - 1) = 3x + 16. Identify and justify each inverse operation.
3 (5 pts). For each equation, decide whether it has one, no, or infinitely many solutions. Explain:
   A. 4(y + 2) = 4y + 8
   B. 3(z + 2) = 3z + 5
4 (5 pts). Solve -4t + 7 ≥ 19. Represent the solution in inequality notation and explain whether t = -3 is included.
5 (10 pts). A fundraiser sells notebooks for $7 each and pays a $25 setup fee. The goal is at least $200 in revenue after paying setup. Define a nonnegative integer n, write an inequality, determine the minimum notebooks needed and check your conclusion. Clearly distinguish sales revenue from net revenue.
Respond to every item. Your teacher will evaluate accuracy, reasoning and communication using the published rubric.

rubricCriteria.label: Expressions and simplification
rubricCriteria.description: Distributive property and combining like terms with accurate reasoning.

rubricCriteria.description: Correct methods, checks and distinction of one/no/all solutions.

rubricCriteria.label: Inequality solving and interpretation
rubricCriteria.description: Correct sign reversals, boundary inclusion and contextual restrictions.

rubricCriteria.label: Modeling and communication
rubricCriteria.description: Clearly defined variables, feasible conclusion and concise explanation.

teacherNotes.diagnostic: Pre-assess arithmetic with negatives and distributive property; reteach if needed.
teacherNotes.accommodations: Read prompts aloud; permit extended time, manipulatives, bilingual glossary and text-to-speech; preserve mathematical rigor.
teacherNotes.differentiation: Provide balance-model manipulatives for emerging learners and parameterized variable problems for advanced learners.
teacherNotes.teacherAnswersOnly: The complete teacher key should remain in teacher-controlled documents, not in student-facing curriculum metadata.
teacherNotes.grading: Formative 20-point practice plus 30-point checkpoint. Completion markers are not grades.
teacherNotes.creditPolicy: This unit alone earns no course credit; credit is determined only after the yearlong course, instructional supervision, student evidence and school approval.
